urgeschichte#summary: From fire through the spread of modern humans to the first farmers and villages: the Stone Age covers the longest stretch of human history.
urgeschichte#overview.0: Prehistory is the period before the invention of writing. Since there are no written sources, we know about it only through bone finds, stone tools, cave paintings, settlement remains, and today also through the analysis of ancient DNA. The Stone Age is named after the most important material used for tools and is divided into the Paleolithic, the Mesolithic, and the Neolithic.
urgeschichte#overview.1: The ancestors of humans evolved in Africa. Early human forms such as Homo erectus learned to control fire and spread as far as Asia and Europe. Anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, emerged around 300,000 years ago in Africa. About 70,000 years ago small groups left the continent and, over the following tens of thousands of years, settled Asia, Australia, Europe, and finally the Americas.
urgeschichte#overview.2: The people of the Paleolithic lived as hunter-gatherers in small, mobile groups. They made tools from stone, bone, and wood, sewed clothing, buried their dead, and created works of art such as the cave paintings of Lascaux or small figures carved from ivory. For a time they shared Europe and Asia with other human species such as the Neanderthals, who died out about 40,000 years ago.
urgeschichte#overview.3: After the end of the last Ice Age, the Neolithic Revolution began around 11,500 years ago in the Fertile Crescent: people started to cultivate grain and to breed animals, and they settled down. This new way of life spread slowly into Europe, Africa, and Asia, and arose independently in China, the Americas, and other regions as well. Villages such as Çatalhöyük emerged, along with pottery, weaving, and larger buildings.
urgeschichte#overview.4: With settled life the population grew, stores were laid up, and possessions became more important. Towards the end of the Neolithic, the working of copper, the plough, and the wheel were added. Out of these innovations the first cities and early civilizations developed around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and with them begins the history recorded in writing.
urgeschichte#consequences.0: Modern humans spread out from Africa to settle every habitable continent and are today the only surviving human species.
urgeschichte#consequences.1: The Neolithic Revolution turned hunter-gatherers into settled farmers and thereby created the basis for villages, cities, and states.
urgeschichte#consequences.2: Farming and animal husbandry made storage, population growth, and the division of labour possible, but also inequality, property, and new diseases.
urgeschichte#consequences.3: Tools, fire, language, art, and religion from the Stone Age remain among the fundamental features of human culture to this day.
urgeschichte#consequences.4: Inventions such as pottery, weaving, the wheel, and metalworking paved the way for the early civilizations of the Bronze Age.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.0: Around 2.6 million years ago early humans in East Africa make the first stone tools (Oldowan).
urgeschichte#keyFacts.1: About 1.8 million years ago Homo erectus becomes the first human species to leave Africa, reaching Asia and Europe.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.2: By 400,000 years ago at the latest, humans use fire regularly; around 300,000 years ago Homo sapiens emerges in Africa.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.3: About 75,000 years ago the oldest known ornaments and decorative beads are produced in Blombos Cave in South Africa.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.4: Around 50,000 years ago humans reach Australia and about 15,000 years ago the Americas; around 1500 BC the settlement of the Pacific islands begins.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.5: From about 9500 BC the Neolithic Revolution begins in the Fertile Crescent, with farming, animal husbandry, and permanent villages such as Jericho.
urgeschichte#keyFacts.6: Around 5000 BC copper working begins; around 3500 BC the wheel, the plough, and the domesticated horse are added.
urgeschichte#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
urgeschichte#sections.0.paragraphs.0: For hundreds of thousands of years people lived in small groups of mostly 20 to 50 individuals in which there were no fixed rulers. Decisions were probably made jointly, and standing rested on experience, success in hunting, or knowledge of plants and remedies. Since hunter-gatherers could carry hardly any possessions with them, differences between people remained small. Archaeology therefore speaks of largely egalitarian societies.
urgeschichte#sections.0.paragraphs.1: With settled life this changed. Stores, fields, herds, and houses could be inherited, and settlements such as Jericho or Çatalhöyük needed rules for water, land, and defence. In the Neolithic, richly furnished graves appear for the first time, showing that individual families had more influence and property than others. Communal structures such as stone circles, burial mounds, or town walls presupposed that someone was able to organize hundreds of people.
urgeschichte#sections.0.paragraphs.2: Towards the end of the Neolithic and in the Copper Age this development intensified. Copper axes, jewellery, and weapons from graves such as the one at Varna in Bulgaria marked rank and power. Village heads and clan leaders became chieftains, and chiefdoms eventually became the first cities and states of Mesopotamia and Egypt.
urgeschichte#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
urgeschichte#sections.1.paragraphs.0: Everyday life in the Paleolithic was shaped by movement: groups followed animal herds, ripening fruit, and the seasons, and lived in caves, under rock shelters, or in tents made of hides and mammoth bones. Women and men shared the work, and gathering plants, nuts, eggs, and small animals often supplied more food than big-game hunting. Children learned by imitation; the old passed on knowledge about tools, paths, and stories.
urgeschichte#sections.1.paragraphs.1: Finds of healed bone fractures and of people in need of care show that the sick and injured were looked after. The dead were buried, often sprinkled with ochre and provided with jewellery or tools, which points to ideas of a life after death. Clothing made of hides was sewn with bone needles; sewing needles are attested from around 40,000 years ago.
urgeschichte#sections.1.paragraphs.2: In the villages of the Neolithic people lived closer together than ever before. Farming meant hard, monotonous work, and skeletons show more wear, tooth decay, and deficiency diseases than among hunter-gatherers. At the same time the number of children rose, because grain porridge shortened the period of breastfeeding. Diseases such as measles or tuberculosis passed from livestock to humans, and stores aroused the envy of neighbours, so that palisades and ditches were built around the villages.
urgeschichte#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
urgeschichte#sections.2.paragraphs.0: Symbolic thinking is older than previously assumed: in Blombos Cave in South Africa, people carved patterns into pieces of ochre 75,000 years ago and made beads from snail shells. In Europe, around 40,000 years ago, the ivory figures of the Swabian Jura were created, among them the Lion Man and the Venus of Hohle Fels, as well as flutes made from bird bones, the oldest known musical instruments.
urgeschichte#sections.2.paragraphs.1: Cave paintings such as those at Chauvet, Lascaux, or Altamira show mainly animals and rarely humans. Scholarship interprets them as part of hunting magic, initiation rites, or shamanism, but this is not certain. Burials with grave goods, animal figures, and the cult buildings of Göbekli Tepe point to ideas of spirits, ancestors, and supernatural forces long before the first temples were built.
urgeschichte#sections.2.paragraphs.2: The knowledge of Stone Age people was practical and extensive: they knew the properties of hundreds of plants, could strike flint with precision, boil adhesive from birch tar, and use the stars for orientation. Megalithic monuments such as Stonehenge or Newgrange are aligned to the solstices and show that the people of the Neolithic observed the course of the year closely. The invention of pottery made it possible to cook and store food, and its decoration today reveals to archaeologists the origin and contacts of the groups.
urgeschichte#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
urgeschichte#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The technology of the Paleolithic developed slowly but steadily: from the simple flakes of the Oldowan through the bifacially worked hand axe of Homo erectus to the fine blades, spear-throwers, harpoons, and bows of Homo sapiens. Every innovation made hunting and food preparation more efficient. Trade already existed as well: shells and obsidian were exchanged over hundreds of kilometres.
urgeschichte#sections.3.paragraphs.1: With farming and animal husbandry an economy arose that could build up stores and produce surpluses. Grain was harvested with flint sickles, stored in granaries, and ground with grinding stones. Sheep and goats supplied milk, wool, and meat, and cattle later pulled the plough. From about 6000 BC irrigation canals in Mesopotamia made even dry areas fertile and allowed for larger villages.
urgeschichte#sections.3.paragraphs.2: In the Copper Age people began to smelt ores and cast metal in moulds. Copper axes, needles, and jewellery were sought-after goods for exchange, but still soft; only bronze solved this problem. The wheel and the cart, the potter's wheel, the loom, and domesticated horses and donkeys changed transport and craft and initiated the transition to the early civilizations.
fruehe-hochkulturen#summary: On the Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus, and the Yellow River the first cities, states, and scripts emerge: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus civilization, and China shape the Bronze Age.
fruehe-hochkulturen#overview.0: Around 3500 BC the first cities in the world emerged in Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Irrigation agriculture produced surpluses that fed priests, craftsmen, merchants, and officials. In order to administer stores, dues, and trade, the Sumerians developed cuneiform. Temples and palaces, kings, laws, and standing armies characterize these early states.
fruehe-hochkulturen#overview.1: On the Nile, around 3100 BC, a king from Upper Egypt united the land into a single kingdom. The pharaohs were regarded as gods on earth and had themselves buried in enormous pyramids. The annual Nile flood made Egypt a rich agricultural land whose culture, with hieroglyphs, mummification, and temple building, remained remarkably stable for almost three millennia.
fruehe-hochkulturen#overview.2: Early civilizations arose in other river valleys as well: in the Indus Valley, around 2500 BC, systematically planned cities such as Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa flourished, with sewerage and standardized measures. In China the Shang dynasty ruled from about 1600 BC, and Chinese writing emerged from its oracle bones. In Mesoamerica the Olmecs laid the foundations of later cultures such as the Maya from 1200 BC onwards.
fruehe-hochkulturen#overview.3: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, gave the epoch its name. It made better weapons and tools possible and promoted long-distance trade, since tin was rare. Rulers such as Sargon of Akkad, Hammurabi of Babylon, or Ramesses II of Egypt created great empires, concluded alliances, and waged wars over trade routes and tribute. The treaty between the Egyptians and the Hittites after the Battle of Kadesh is the oldest surviving peace treaty.
fruehe-hochkulturen#overview.4: Around 1200 BC many empires of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed within a few decades. Droughts, earthquakes, revolts, and attacks by the so-called Sea Peoples contributed to this. With the end of the Bronze Age the Iron Age began, in which new peoples such as the Phoenicians, Israelites, Assyrians, and Greeks determined the course of history.
fruehe-hochkulturen#consequences.0: With writing, history proper begins: administration, laws, literature, and knowledge could now be recorded permanently.
fruehe-hochkulturen#consequences.1: Cities, states, kings, officials, taxes, and armies arose in this period and shape political order to this day.
fruehe-hochkulturen#consequences.2: Collections of laws such as the Code of Hammurabi established the idea that law should be set down in writing and publicly known.
fruehe-hochkulturen#consequences.3: The astronomy, mathematics, calendars, medicine, and architecture of the early civilizations were taken over by the Greeks, the Romans, and later cultures.
fruehe-hochkulturen#consequences.4: The scripts of Egypt, Mesopotamia, and China became the forerunners of the alphabets and writing systems used worldwide today.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.0: Around 3200 BC cuneiform emerges in Uruk; around 3100 BC a pharaoh unites Upper and Lower Egypt.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.1: Around 2600 BC city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash, and Kish compete in Sumer; their kings lie with rich grave goods in the Royal Tombs of Ur.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.2: The Epic of Gilgamesh, transmitted on clay tablets from about 2100 BC, is humanity's oldest great work of literature.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.3: Between 2000 and 1200 BC the palaces of the Minoans on Crete and of the Mycenaeans in Greece flourish, the first early civilizations of Europe.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.4: From about 1650 BC the Hittites rule Anatolia from Hattusa and become Egypt's great rival.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.5: Around 1200 BC many empires collapse; afterwards iron and the Phoenician alphabet of 22 letters come into general use.
fruehe-hochkulturen#keyFacts.6: From about 900 BC new powers emerge: the Neo-Assyrian Empire, the Kingdom of Kush in Nubia, and the Chavín culture in Peru.
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.0.paragraph: The kings of the early civilizations derived their power from the gods. In Sumer the ruler was regarded as the deputy of the city god, to whom the temple and a large part of the land belonged; the pharaoh of Egypt was himself venerated as a god on earth, as the son of the sun god Ra and the embodiment of Horus. This religious justification made rule stable, but it also obliged the king to secure order, justice, and fertility.

Out of the city-states of Sumer, which fought each other over water and border land, territorial empires arose under Sargon of Akkad and later Hammurabi of Babylon, with governors, messengers, and tax lists. Administration rested on writing: scribes recorded harvests, dues, workers, and rations on thousands of clay tablets. In Egypt a vizier directed the officials of the provinces on behalf of the pharaoh, and in the Middle Kingdom a broad class of educated administrative officials emerged.

In the 2nd millennium BC a system of states took shape, made up of great powers such as Egypt, the Hittites, Babylon, Mitanni, and Assyria, which dealt with one another through envoys, letters in the Akkadian language, gifts, and marriage alliances. The Amarna letters and the treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III attest to this early diplomacy. After the collapse around 1200 BC, the Assyrians, using deportations, provinces, and a standing army, established the first empire to rule the entire Near East.
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.1.paragraph: The societies of the early civilizations were strictly ordered. At the top stood the king, the priests, and high officials, below them scribes, merchants, and craftsmen; the great majority were peasants who worked the land of the temples, palaces, or large landowners and paid dues. Slaves, mostly prisoners of war or debtors, stood at the very bottom, but played a smaller role in the economy than they later did in Greece and Rome.

Women in Egypt had comparatively many rights: they could own property, conclude contracts, bring suits in court, and engage in trade. Individual women such as Hatshepsut even ruled as pharaoh, Nefertiti and Fu Hao exercised great influence, and Enheduanna led an important temple as high priestess. In Mesopotamia the Code of Hammurabi regulated marriage, dowry, divorce, and inheritance in detail; women of the upper class could work as priestesses or businesswomen, but were subordinate to their father or husband.

Everyday life for the majority took place in mudbrick houses with an inner courtyard. People ate bread, onions, lentils, dates, and fish, drank beer brewed from barley, and wine was a luxury. Children of the upper class spent years learning cuneiform or hieroglyphs in scribal schools, while peasant children helped in the fields. Festivals in honour of the gods, such as the New Year festival in Babylon or the Opet festival in Thebes, interrupted the working year and brought the whole city together.
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.2.paragraph: The religions of the early civilizations knew many gods, who were responsible for natural forces, cities, and areas of life: Enlil, Inanna, and Marduk in Mesopotamia, Ra, Osiris, and Isis in Egypt, the weather god among the Hittites. Temples such as the ziggurat of Ur or the temple of Karnak were at once the dwelling of the gods, an economic enterprise, and a centre of learning. The Egyptians believed in a continued life after death, which required mummification, grave goods, and the judgement of the dead before Osiris.

With writing, literature came into being. The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of friendship, the fear of death, and a great flood; Egyptian texts such as the Story of Sinuhe, love songs, and wisdom teachings were copied out over centuries. Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, composed hymns and is the first author known by name in the world. Around 1050 BC the Phoenicians simplified writing into an alphabet of 22 consonant signs, which the Greeks, the Romans, and later almost the entire world adopted.

The science of the early civilizations arose out of practical needs. Babylonian priests observed the stars and planets, predicted lunar eclipses, and created the division of the circle into 360 degrees and of the hour into 60 minutes. Egyptian physicians described wounds and remedies in papyri, surveyors recalculated the fields after every Nile flood, and the Egyptian calendar of 365 days became the model for our own.
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
fruehe-hochkulturen#sections.3.paragraph: The basis of the early civilizations was an agriculture that, thanks to irrigation and river silt, produced high surpluses. In Mesopotamia the canals had to be maintained constantly, because salinization threatened the fields; in Egypt the Nile flood governed the rhythm of sowing and harvest. The plough, the sickle, the donkey, and cattle, and in the Middle Kingdom also water-lifting devices and the Fayum project for reclaiming land, increased yields.

Bronze, made of copper and tin, was the decisive material for weapons, tools, and cult vessels, yet tin was rare and came from Anatolia, Iran, or Afghanistan. Trade routes therefore stretched over thousands of kilometres: lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, cedar wood from Lebanon, gold and ivory from Nubia, copper from Cyprus. The Uluburun shipwreck off the Turkish coast, dating from around 1300 BC, carried goods from at least seven regions.

Long-distance trade lay in the hands of merchants such as the Assyrians, who ran trading colonies in Anatolia, or the Phoenicians, who sailed the entire Mediterranean with their ships and founded colonies such as Carthage. Payment was made in weighed silver, grain, or copper; coins did not yet exist. After 1200 BC iron came into general use; it was more laborious to smelt, but its ore occurred almost everywhere and made tools and weapons affordable for many.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#summary: Long before Europeans crossed the Atlantic, the peoples of the Americas, without contact with the rest of the world, created cities, empires, writing systems and calendars – from the Olmecs and the Maya through the Andean cultures to the mound cities of North America, the Aztecs and the Inca.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#overview.0: After the double continent had been settled during the Ice Age, the people of the Americas developed their own forms of agriculture and civilization independently of Asia, Africa and Europe. In Mexico maize, beans and squash were domesticated, in the Andes potatoes, quinoa and cotton, and people kept llamas and alpacas. Around 1200 BC the Olmecs built the first ceremonial centers of Mesoamerica on the Gulf coast of Mexico, and in the Andes Chavín de Huántar became a far-reaching cult site from about 900 BC. At the same time, hunter-gatherers at Poverty Point on the lower Mississippi raised enormous earthworks.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#overview.1: Over the following centuries, cities with pyramids, plazas and ball courts arose in Mesoamerica. The Zapotecs founded Monte Albán around 500 BC, and the Maya built city-states such as El Mirador, Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque in the lowlands of Guatemala and Yucatán, developing a complete writing system and a highly precise calendar. Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico, with perhaps 100,000 inhabitants around AD 500, was one of the largest cities in the world. In the 9th century the Classic Maya cities of the south declined, while Chichén Itzá rose in the north and Tula, the city of the Toltecs, in central Mexico.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#overview.2: In the Andes, Chavín was followed by regional cultures such as Paracas and Nazca on the south coast and the Moche on the north coast of Peru, famous for irrigation canals, goldsmithing and pottery. Between AD 500 and 1000 Tiwanaku on Lake Titicaca and the Wari empire dominated large parts of the highlands, and later the kingdom of Chimú with its adobe capital Chan Chan ruled the coast. From about 1438 Pachacuti and his successors turned the small realm of Cusco into the Inca empire of Tawantinsuyu, which stretched from Ecuador to Chile and was administered through roads, storehouses and knotted cords. With probably around ten million subjects, it was the largest empire in the Americas around 1500.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#overview.3: Beyond the great empires, North and South America were also densely settled and diverse. The Hopewell culture in the Ohio Valley maintained an exchange network across half the continent, Cahokia on the Mississippi was the largest city north of Mexico around 1100, and the Ancestral Puebloans built multistory great houses in Chaco Canyon. In the northeast five peoples joined together in the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, in the Caribbean the Taíno lived in chiefdoms, and in the Amazon basin mounds, causeways and fertile dark earth bear witness to large settled societies. These cultures left no writing, but archaeology and the oral traditions of their descendants reveal their history.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#overview.4: In 1428 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed the Aztec Triple Alliance, which soon made large parts of Mexico pay tribute. Around 1500, according to modern estimates, many millions of people lived in the Americas, most of them in Mesoamerica and the Andes. The arrival of Columbus in 1492 began contact with Europe, and introduced diseases often spread faster than the conquerors themselves. The destruction of the Aztec empire in 1521 and the capture of the Inca Atahualpa in 1532 ended the era of the independent great empires, but not the peoples, languages and traditions of the Americas.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.0: Plants domesticated in the Americas – maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, squash, peppers, cacao and tobacco – transformed the diet and agriculture of the whole world after 1492.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.1: Maya writing is one of the few independently invented writing systems of humankind; its decipherment in the 20th century has made the history of the Maya kings readable again.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.2: Millions of people today speak Maya languages, Quechua, Aymara, Nahuatl and other Indigenous languages; festivals, crafts, farming and religious beliefs preserve much of the pre-Columbian heritage.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.3: Ruined sites such as Teotihuacan, Tikal, Chichén Itzá, Machu Picchu, Cahokia and Chaco Canyon are UNESCO World Heritage Sites and shape the self-image of Mexico, Peru and other countries.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.4: The order of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, with its council and the say of the clan mothers, is still discussed today as an early example of a federal constitution in the Americas.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#consequences.5: New methods such as airborne laser scanning show that rainforests in Central America and Amazonia were also densely settled, changing the picture of an "untouched" America before 1492.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.0: Around 1200 BC the Olmec center of San Lorenzo arises, and from about 900 BC La Venta and the cult site of Chavín de Huántar in the Andes.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.1: Around 500 BC the Zapotecs found Monte Albán; in 36 BC a stela at Chiapa de Corzo bears the oldest known Long Count date.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.2: Around AD 500 Teotihuacan, with perhaps 100,000 inhabitants, is the largest city in the Americas.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.3: From 615 to 683 Pakal rules in Palenque; in 909 the last known Long Count date is carved at Toniná.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.4: Around 1100 Cahokia on the Mississippi, with Monks Mound, is the largest settlement north of Mexico.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.5: In 1325 the Mexica found Tenochtitlan; in 1428 they form the Aztec Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#keyFacts.6: From about 1438 Pachacuti builds the Inca empire; around 1527 Huayna Capac dies, and a war between brothers weakens the empire shortly before the Spaniards arrive.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.0.paragra: For centuries Mesoamerica was a world of rival city-states. The Maya kings bore the title "holy lord", traced their descent to gods and ancestors and had their deeds recorded on stelae and altars. Great powers such as Tikal and Calakmul formed systems of alliances with dependent cities and waged wars lasting decades, in which captured lords were often sacrificed. In the 4th century Teotihuacan even intervened in the royal succession of Tikal, which shows the far-reaching connections within Mesoamerica.

The Aztecs, who called themselves Mexica, came to the Valley of Mexico as migrants in the 13th century and founded Tenochtitlan in 1325. After defeating the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, they formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan in 1428. The empire did not consist of tightly administered provinces but of subject cities that kept their own rulers but had to deliver tribute regularly in the form of maize, cotton cloth, cacao, feathers and gold. At its head stood the tlatoani, who was chosen by a council from within the noble family.

The Inca empire, by contrast, was a tightly organized state. The Inca was regarded as the son of the sun; under him were four parts of the empire, provinces and an administration organized in groups of ten. Conquered peoples had to perform labor service, whole population groups were resettled to prevent revolts, and Quechua became the language of administration. Because there was no fixed rule of succession, changes of ruler often led to power struggles, most recently in the war between the brothers Huáscar and Atahualpa.

No great empires arose in North America, but a variety of political orders did. Cahokia was the center of a chiefdom with a hereditary elite that held sway over thousands of people. In the northeast the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, according to their tradition, agreed on the Great Law of Peace: a joint council of chiefs decided by consensus, and the clan mothers determined who held these offices. In the Caribbean, caciques, among them women, ruled over villages and alliances on the large islands.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.1.paragra: Agriculture was the basis of almost all societies. In Mesoamerica families grew maize, beans and squash together in one field; maize flatbreads and beans were the daily food, and cacao was a drink of the upper class. In the Andes terraces were built on steep slopes, and potatoes were freeze-dried by frost and sun into long-lasting chuño. Domestic animals were rare: in Mesoamerica people kept turkeys and dogs, in the Andes llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs.

Societies were usually strictly stratified. Above farmers and craftsmen stood nobles, priests and warriors, and at the top a ruler with divine dignity. Among the Aztecs the calpolli, neighborhood associations, formed the basic unit; they distributed land, organized labor service and maintained schools for young men. Long-distance traders, the pochteca, enjoyed rights of their own. In the Inca empire the ayllu, a kin group with common land, was the core cell of village and state.

Women played an important role in many cultures. They prepared food, wove cloth that served as tribute and a store of value, and worked as traders in the markets. Among the Maya, queens such as Lady Six Sky ruled at Naranjo, and the tomb of the Lady of Cao shows that among the Moche, too, women held the highest offices. In the Inca empire chosen women, the acllas, wove the finest cloth for rulers and temples in houses of their own, and among the Haudenosaunee the clan mothers held great political influence.

The great cities presented a lively picture. Tenochtitlan, with perhaps 200,000 inhabitants, was crisscrossed by canals on which canoes carried goods, and the market in the district of Tlatelolco later impressed the Spanish conquerors. In Teotihuacan families lived in large apartment compounds, including separate neighborhoods for migrants from Oaxaca and the Maya region. The Mesoamerican ball game, in which a heavy rubber ball could only be moved with the hips and body, was sport, ritual and political event all at once.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
